title: Bulk electrical power extraction through tunnel transmission technology from renewable energy concentrated zones

paper_content.abstract:
Mountainous regions, such as the Alps, Appalachians, Andes, and Qingzang Plateau, offer
vast renewable energy potential, but geographical and ecological challenges limit conventional
overhead transmission lines. Underground alternatives, including gas-insulated lines and cables,
provide viable solutions but require comprehensive techno-economic evaluation for sustainable
deployment. This study integrates multi-physics analysis, combining electromagnetic, thermal,
and fluid dynamics, with lifecycle cost assessment per unit transmission task to compare
overhead and underground tunnel transmission systems. Optimized conductor designs and
ventilation strategies enhance cable capacity and improvRe economic performance, particularly in
regions with high external costs. Here, we sh ow that underground tunnel based power
transmission systems, especially gas-insulIated lines, deliver cost-effective, high-capacity
transmission solutions for mountainous renewable energy concentrated regions, outperform
overhead power transmission infrastructure when external costs, including ecological, landscape,
and infrastructure constraRints, are significant, thus advancing the goals of sustainable renewable
energy integration and net-zero.
paper_content.introduction:
Facing the global energy crisis and increasing urgency of transitioning towards a low-
carbon future1,2, effective utilization of renewable energy has become crucial. By 2027, the global
renewable energy generation capacity is projected to increase by approximately 2,400 GW3. The
capacity and type of renewable energy construction expected to be completed by 2027 in
countries/regions around the world is provided in Supplementary Figure 1. A critical challenge
in realizing this growth lies in transmitting power from remote, resource-rich regions to demand
centers, ensuring feasibility, stability, and alignment with environmental policies and public
expectations4.
Untapped renewable energy resources are particularly concentrated in mountainous and
highland regions5,6, where elevated terrain enhances solar irradiance7, wind speeds8, and
hydropower potential. Other areas, such as offshore wind sites, also represent globally significant
resources, but the present study focuses on mountainous and plateau regions where corridor
scarcity and ecological sensitivity are especially pronounced. However, these areas frequently
overlap with ecologically sensitive or scenic regions9,10. For example, the Appalachian Mountains
in eastern North America hold an estimated 1,859 GW of wind power generation capacity
potential11, while the Andes in South America possess about 243 GW of combined wind and
geothermal generation capacity potential12. The NEuropean Alps offer 19.9 GW of wind generation
capacity potential, 45 GW of solar generat ion capacity potential, and 8.56 GW of hydropower
generation capacity potential8. In Chin L a, the Qingzang Plateau is targeted for the development of
227 GW of hydropower generation capacity and 96 GW of photovoltaic generation capacity13–15.
Indonesia’s Central Range (New Guinea Highlands) contains approximately 26 GW of renewable
generation capacity potential, most of which is hydropower, leveraging the area’s rugged terrain16.
These figures, which are shown in Table 1, are based on regional studies that report only partial,
technically proven reserves rather than the full exploitable potential of each mountain range.
Although the methodologies differ—ranging from geographic information system-based spatial
analysis to hydrological modeling—they consistently highlight the vast untapped renewable
potential of these regions17,18.
However, transmitting renewable energy from these areas faces significant challenges:
Geographical and Corridor Constraints: Mountainous regions require long-distance exports to
lowland load centers, yet feasible overhead corridors are sharply limited by rugged terrain and
regulatory siting restrictions. On the Qingzang Plateau, for instance, four planned transmission
pathways (northern, southern, central, and central-branch) intersect with multiple nature reserves,
leaving only ~16 feasible HV circuits compared to ~37 required for the planned renewable
buildout (≈40% realizable via OHL)19,20. Comparable potential corridor scarcity exists in the
Alps, where Natura 2000 and UNESCO sites restrict routing options, and in the Appalachians,
where national forests and the Appalachian Trail limit siting flexibility. Ecological and Tourism
Protection: Beyond technical siting limits, these mountain regions also carry exceptional
ecological and scenic value21. Overhead lines fragment habitats and impair landscapes, triggering
strong public opposition. In the Alps, willingness-to-pay (WTP) studies indicate more than
$900,000 per kilometer per year to undergroun d lines, reflecting the premium placed on
preserving biodiversity and visual integrity 22,23.
For decades, traditional overLhead transmission lines (OHL) have dominated power
delivery, yet they inadequately address these challenges in renewable-rich mountainous and
plateau scenarios. This Rhas spurred exploration of alternatives, with underground tunnel
transmission emerging as a viable solution for long-distance, high-capacity power transport.
Unlike OHL, tunnels bypass surface constraints and ecological impacts, enabling delivery
through challenging terrains while preserving landscapes24,25. The undergrounding alternatives
include direct-buried and tunnel installations; while direct burial is generally cheaper, in
mountainous, corridor-scarce, and environmentally sensitive segments, continuous trenching is
often infeasible and operators therefore typically adopt accessible cable tunnels for bulk
transmission25.
However, applying underground transmission tunnel technologies—such as cross-linked
polyethylene (XLPE) AC or DC cables or higher-voltage gas-insulated lines (GIL)—to
renewable-rich regions presents multiple unresolved challenges26. First, economic costs are a
primary concern. Although, studies have quantified the additional ecological and landscape costs
of overhead transmission lines (OHLs) and the economic benefits of undergrounding, clear
criteria and guidelines for determining which regions should prioritize underground solutions
versus OHLs, based on regional characteristics, remain absent. Second, the design of current-
carrying capacity for lines within tunnels has been evaluated by finite element analysis,
accounting for electromagnetic and thermal coupling27–30. However, few studies have
investigated how the spatial arrangement of lines within tunnels impacts their current-carrying
capacity31. Third, ventilation is critical for maintaining eRnvironmental stability in long, confined
tunnel spaces. Previous research has proposed vent ilation strategies for cable tunnels using finite
element analysis32, and a recent study oIptimized ventilation by constraining conductor
temperatures and factoring in energy loss costs33,34. However, this work was limited to a single-
tunnel scenario and focused solely on reducing ventilation energy losses, without exploring the
coupled relationship between ventilation and current-carrying capacity in long-distance tunnels.
Furthermore, current research has not sufficiently elucidated the interplay between multi-physics
fields—encompassing electromagnetic, thermal, and fluid dynamics—and economic benefits in
critical tunnel design aspects, such as line layout and ventilation. This gap hinders the
development of comprehensive design guidelines and economic evaluation frameworks for long-
distance tunnel transmission in mountainous regions.
In this work, we present a comprehensive framework for evaluating underground tunnel
transmission in renewable-rich mountainous and plateau scenarios, delivering three key
contributions: (1) A multi-physics coupling methodology integrating electromagnetic-thermal-
fluid finite element analysis with annualized lifecycle cost (LCC) per unit transmission task
(MW-km) evaluation, enabling rigorous comparison of GIL, UGC AC, and UGC DC under
realistic constraints. (2) A techno-economic model that accounts for ecological and landscape
costs, demonstrating that underground solutions, particularly GIL, achieve lower annualized LCC
per unit transmission task (MW-km) than overhead lines when external costs exceed
$550,000/km/year, redefining economic feasibility for renewable energy transmission in
mountainous regions worldwide. (3) Quantitative insights into spatial and ventilation
optimizations, demonstrating up to 57% capacity enhancements (e.g., AC cables from 1,273 A to
2,003 A) and 20% LCC savings in annualized LCC per unit transmission task (MW-km) via
parameterized simulations, providing actionable design gRuidelines for sustainable energy delivery.
This framework equips policymakers and engineers with a decision-support matrix, accelerating
deployment of underground tunnels to uInlock mountainous renewables, foster net-zero
transitions, and balance economic, environmental, and social imperatives.

Comparative Techno-Economic Evaluation of Transmission Technologies for Renewable
Energy Concentrated Zones
To evaluate the economic viability of various high-capacity power transmission methods,
we analyzed alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) overhead lines (OHL), underground
tunnel AC cables (UGC AC), and gas-insulated lines (GIL).
We selected 500 kV AC and ±600 kV DC overhead lines as benchmarks, as these are
widely adopted and technologically mature transmission systems. Cost data for these lines were
sourced from the 2024 MISO handbook, which provides U.S. power infrastructure construction
costs, with the tower type specified as an angled dead-end structure, suitable for mountainous
and high-altitude regions rich in renewable energy35. While China has implemented mature 1,000
kV AC and ±1,000 kV DC overhead lines with estimated costs of approximately $3,802,580/km
and $1,801,444/km, respectively, these data stem from specific projects and the technologies are
less commonly applied globally36. Thus, they are excluded from the main analysis but provided
in Supplementary Table 1 for reference.
For underground tunnel AC transmission, construction costs were derived from the 2025
IET report on underground cable systems37. Because published cost data for long tunnel GIL
systems remain scarce, we explicitly note that the Su-Tong GIL corridor is a short river-crossing
tunnel (Yangtze crossing) and use it as a conservative reference , while Supplementary Tables 1–
2 compile additional project data (including an Chinese GRIL tunnel) to broaden the evidence base.
Operation and maintenance costs were estimated based on industry averages and multiple
research reports. The Su-Tong GIL project haIs a rated current of 6,300 A. However, based on a
State Grid Corporation of China report and our subsequent studies38, dual-circuit lines operate at
a reduced current of 3,150 A under normal conditions to maintain stable tunnel temperatures.
Therefore, the capacity calculations are based on 3,150 A. Energy loss data for AC and DC
overhead lines were obtained from EIA report39. For UGC AC and GIL, where empirical loss
data are scarce, we conducted coupled electromagnetic-thermal-fluidic finite element analysis,
estimating energy losses of 11.91%/1,000 km for UGC AC and 6.71%/1,000 km for GIL
(Calculation details are shown in the Methods Section). These numbers align closely with
industry expectations and also with the data we collected from State Grid Corporation of China,
which is 15.2%/1,000 km and 5.96%/1,000 km for UGC AC and GIL, respectively. The data are
given in Supplementary Table 2.
Transmission lines in renewable-rich mountainous regions often traverse ecologically
sensitive or scenic areas, where OHLs significantly impact ecosystems and aesthetic value40. To
quantify these costs, we adopted the willingness-to-pay (WTP) metric, using the Alps as a case.
Two studies reported residents’ WTP for undergrounding overhead lines in the Alps at
$984,000/year/km and $892,043/year/km, respectively. We used their average, $938,022/year/km,
for cost estimation22,41.
Although we also investigated underground DC transmission, limited case studies and
data availability constrained the cost analysis. However, we posit that its costs are comparable to
underground AC cables, as both primarily incur additional expenses from tunnel construction and
equipment installation compared to overhead lines.
Table 2 summarizes the economic cost data for thRese transmission methods. Although the
data are drawn from diverse countries, projects, and studies, it still serves a reliable reference for
comparative analysis.
To determine the most suitable transmission method for renewable energy-rich regions,
we evaluated lifecycle unit capacity costs, analyzing total and per-unit-length costs as a function
of transmission distance, which is shown in Fig. 1.
Ecological and landscape costs constitute a significant portion of overhead line expenses,
particularly in sensitive regions like the Alps. These costs vary by region, so we plotted cost
curves with and without ecological considerations. When including ecological costs, overhead
lines exhibit the highest lifecycle unit costs: approximately $430/year/MW/km (DC) and
$400/year/MW/km (AC) at a 500 km distance. Underground AC cables follow at
$321/year/MW/km, and GIL at $263/year/MW/km.
Excluding ecological costs, overhead lines are significantly cheaper, with costs of
$33/year/MW/km (DC) and $28/year/MW/km (AC). Thus, without ecological costs, GIL costs
are roughly 8 times higher than overhead lines, and costs for underground AC cables are
approximately ten times higher. When ecological costs are excluded, overhead AC lines are more
cost-effective for distances below 800 km, while DC lines become preferable beyond 800 km.
This aligns with trends in prior studies42.
Acknowledging that infrastructure costs—particularly tunnel excavation—are highly
project-specific and dependent on local geological conditions, we conducted a comprehensive
sensitivity analysis to validate the robustness of our economic model. We evaluated the impact
of cost variations across three key dimensions: tunnel civil engineering costs (ranging from −50%
to +100% to cover geological complexities), electrical equipment costs, and operation and
maintenance expenses43. The detailed parameter settinRgs and the resulting sensitivity analysis
(presented as a tornado diagram) are provided in Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary
Figure 2. The results demonstrate that the Ieconomic advantage of GIL is resilient to cost
uncertainties; even under scenarios of significantly higher tunnel construction costs (e.g., in
complex terrain), the GIL system remains a cost-competitive alternative to overhead lines when
high ecological externalities are factored in.
The choice between overhead and underground solutions hinges on ecological, landscape,
and other external costs, such as additional expenses for constructing new lines in fully occupied
corridors, forest clearing, ecological fees, and steep terrain construction. Further analysis reveals
that when these external costs reach $550,000/km/year, overhead lines’ unit costs approach those
of GIL; at $720,000/km/year, they align with underground AC cables. Therefore, we conclude
that underground GIL systems become more cost-effective when external costs exceed
$550,000/km/year in target regions, offering a viable alternative for sustainable, high-capacity
power transmission.
Electromagnetic Safety Analysis of Transmission Technologies in Underground Tunnels
Electromagnetic safety is a critical consideration for underground tunnels housing high-
voltage equipment. The confined geometry and proximity of conductors, maintenance personnel,
and surrounding infrastructure necessitate rigorous evaluation of electric and magnetic field
distributions to ensure operational safety and compliance with regulations44.
Following IEEE standards, occupational exposure limits for 50 Hz AC magnetic fields
are 2,710 μT and electric fields are 5 kV/m; for DC, magnetic fields are limited to 353,000 μT
and electric fields are limited to 5 kV/m (based on stricter head-exposure criteria)45,46. ICNIRP
standards limit electric fields to 10 kV/m and magnetic fields to 1,000 μT for AC 50Hz47. For this
analysis, we adopt the stricter standards: AC (50 Hz): 5 kV/m, 1,000 μT; DC: 5 kV/m, 353,000
μT.
For electric fields, both XLPE cablIes (AC and DC) and gas-insulated lines (GIL)
incorporate grounded shielding layers or enclosures, resulting in external electric fields near zero
during normal operation. However, it is crucial to distinguish normal operation from fault
conditions. While the aRforementioned shielding is effective under steady-state scenarios,
insulation breakdowns—though relatively infrequent with typical failure rates of approximately
0.1 to 0.5 failures per 100 km·year for modern high-voltage systems —pose a different set of
risks. In the event of an insulation fault, short-circuit currents (often reaching tens of kA) will
flow through the cable sheath. Without proper mitigation, this massive current induces significant
longitudinal voltages along the sheath, creating life-threatening touch potentials at the cable
surface. To mitigate this risk, we recommend the installation of Sheath Voltage Limiters (SVLs)
within the system—typically at cross-bonding points—to clamp potential overvoltages to safe
levels. Additionally, implementing an equipotential grounding grid throughout the tunnel is
advised. These measures ensure that the tunnel environment remains safe for maintenance
personnel access.
A more common scenario involves partially grounded shielding due to distant grounding
points. Simulations indicate that with a shielding layer voltage of approximately 1 V, the electric
field at 0.1 m from the conductor is about 3.76 V/m, well below safety thresholds. These
simulation results are detailed in Supplementary Figure 3. For these simulations, excitation
voltages were 500 kV (AC XLPE), 500 kV (DC XLPE), and 1,000 kV (GIL), with currents of
2,000 A (AC), 2,000 A (DC), and 6,000 A (GIL). Thus, electric field intensities and touch
potentials in tunnels are controllable and safe through the combination of conductor shielding
and fault protection measures.
Magnetic field analysis is complex due to the influence of multi-phase conductor
arrangements and shielding interconnection mIethods. We conducted magnetic field simulations
in tunnel environments, evaluating AC and DC cables in circular and square tunnels with stacked
and wall-mounted configurations (see Supplementary Figure 4 for schematics and dimensions).
For GIL, we analyzed the tunnel configuration of the Su-Tong GIL corridor 38 (Supplementary
Figure 5).
Regarding shielding grounding methods, DC cable shielding does not produce induced
voltage due to the absence of time-varying currents, allowing solid bonding48. GIL enclosures,
designed as continuous conductors to carry the return current, significantly reduce external
magnetic fields and transmission losses, typically employing solid bonding or multiple-point
bonding rather than cross-bonding. In contrast, long-distance AC XLPE cables, due to high
shielding losses, generally use cross-bonding. In our tunnel model simulations, DC cable
shielding and GIL enclosures use solid bonding, while AC cable shielding employs cross-bonding.
Magnetic field intensity distributions in tunnel environments are shown in Fig. 2.
In tunnels, GIL exhibits the lowest external magnetic field intensity, posing no health risks
unless directly contacting the conductor surface. DC cables produce higher magnetic fields,
approximately 500 μT within 0.6 m, but these remain well below the DC safety limit of 353,000
μT. AC cables show significantly higher magnetic fields, exceeding 1,000 μT within a 0.3 m
radius for both stacked and wall-mounted configurations. Simulation results suggest that wall-
mounted configurations allow maintenance personnel to avoid high-intensity magnetic fields in
the tunnel’s central walkway. For stacked configurations, placing conductors entirely along
tunnel walls is preferable to minimize exposure.
Spatial Configuration Effects on Power Loss and Thermal Performance in Underground
Tunnels
The operation of transmission syste ms in tunnel environments differs significantly from
overhead lines due to the confined, elongated space with limited heat dissipation49. A primary
challenge is balancing increased current-carrying capacity—enhancing economic value—with
the pronounced thermal effects it induces. Excessive heat, causing conductor temperatures to
exceed 90°C for XLPE cables (or 105°C for GIL)38, reduces conductor lifespan. Variations in
conductor spatial arrangements influence power loss and temperature through magnetic field
coupling and altered heat dissipation structures. To investigate these effects, we conducted finite
element analysis on the impact of conductor spatial arrangements on temperature and power loss
for three tunnel configurations.
We defined spatial parameters based on installation methods: for stacked cable
configurations, L represents the distance between the centers of two circuits; for GIL, L
denotes the horizontal distance between circuits. In square wall-mounted and GIL scenarios, H
indicates the vertical distance between adjacent conductors within the same circuit. In circular
wall-mounted scenarios,  represents the angle between the line connecting the topmost
conductor to the tunnel center and the horizontal axis. These parameters are illustrated in
Supplementary Figure 4. The resulting conductor temperature variations and tunnel thermal
losses are shown in Fig. 3.
For AC cables in stacked configurations with fixed intra-phase distances, increasing the
inter-circuit distance (L) has minimal impact on power loss but reduces conductor temperature.
In circular stacked scenarios, total losses increase slightly from 345 W/m (L = 0.4 m) to 347
W/m ( L = 1.4 m), while temperature decreases from 131.02°C to 126.42°C. In square stacked
scenarios, losses rise from 338 W/m ( L = 0.4 m) to 344 W/m ( L = 1.5 m), with temperature
dropping from 125.41°C to 121.86°C. This indicates that increasing the distance between heat
sources slightly increases losses (primarily shielding layer losses, with conductor losses
unchanged) but enhances heat dissipation, lowering conductor temperature and slightly
increasing current-carrying capacity from 1,273 A to 1,304 A (circular) and 1,310 A to 1,335 A
(square). In wall-mounted configurations, increasing intra-circuit conductor distance
significantly reduces shielding layer losses, from 64 W/m to 2 W/m (circular) and 88 W/m to 3
W/m (square), boosting current-carrying capacity by over 200 A in both scenarios. Further
analysis attributes this to the cross-bonding shielding method used, where larger intra-phase
distances allow balanced three-phase induced currents to neutralize shielding layer currents,
reducing losses. For AC cables, I²R losses dominate across all configurations. In stacked
configurations, shielding layer losses are significant (64–88 W/m, ~18–25% of total losses of
338–347 W/m), despite mitigation by cross-bonding. In wall-mounted configurations, shielding
layer losses drop to 2–3 W/m, making I²R losses even more dominant. AC cables exhibit higher
I²R losses than DC cables due to two factors: (1) shielding layer losses increase conductor
temperature, raising resistance, and (2) skin effect increases effective conductor resistance.
Simulations using a uniform multi-turn conductor model (single turn) estimate I²R losses without
skin effect at 168.37 W/m, compared to 235.63 W/m with skin effect, indicating a skin effect
contribution of ~67.26 W/m (~19% of stacked losses, ~32% of minimum wall-mounted losses).
Note that skin effect is a component of I²R losses, manifesting as increased resistance.
For DC cables, the static magnetic field eliminates shielding layer induced currents and
associated thermal losses, as well as AC-specific skin effects, resulting in lower losses and
temperatures compared to AC cables, unaffected by spatial arrangement. However, increasing
heat source distance improves dissipation, slightly raisiRng current-carrying capacity from 2,605
A, 2,658 A, 2,655 A, and 2,668 A to 2,663 A, 2,6 84 A, 2,714 A, and 2,710 A across the four
scenarios, with increases ranging from 26 A tIo 59 A. For DC cables, I²R losses are the sole loss
mechanism, as shielding layer losses and skin effect are absent.
For GIL, prior magnetic environment analysis shows low external magnetic fields and
minimal inter-phase coupling due to larger line distances, resulting in negligible power loss
changes with spatial arrangement. Capacity increases, driven by improved heat dissipation from
increased L and H , are modest, from 4,411 A to 4,466 A. For GIL, I²R losses dominate (976–
991 W/m, ~70–72% of total losses), with enclosure losses (386–394 W/m, ~28%) also significant,
aligning with the data from a Sutong GIL related reference50. Skin effect contributes ~11% of
total losses, as estimated using the same multi-turn conductor model.
Overall, increasing inter-conductor distance and adopting wall-mounted configurations
significantly enhance AC cable current-carrying capacity, reducing power loss and allowing
increases from 1,273 A to 2,003 A under temperature constraints. For DC cables, the absence of
induced currents limits the impact of spatial changes, and for GIL, low external fields and large
distances minimize loss variations, with capacity gains primarily from improved heat dissipation.
These findings provide a clear guidance for tunnel based power transmission design for
renewable energy dispatch from energy concentrated zones.
Simulations assumed cross-bonded grounding and balanced three-phase currents. With
unbalanced currents, AC cable shielding losses increase. In circular stacked and wall-mounted
scenarios, with phase angles of 0°, ±90°, and 0°, ±60°, shielding losses in stacked configurations
rise from 109 W/m to 144 W/m (0°, ±90°) and 248 W/m (0°, ±60°), and in wall-mounted
configurations from 22 W/m to 37 W/m (0°, ±90°) and 149 W/m (0°, ±60°), which is shown in
Supplementary Figure 6. This significantly reduces cRurrent-carrying capacity, particularly in
stacked scenarios.

paper_content.methods:
Lifecycle cost analysis
To assess the economic viability of powerP transmission systems, we calculated the
construction costs of transmission lines and substations separately. For new lines, we assumed
the need for substations or converter stations at both ends to match the line’s capacity.
For 500 kV AC and ±600 kV DC overhead lines, construction and substation/converter
station costs, including operation and maintenance, were sourced from the 2024 MISO report35.
For AC substations, the report requires additional parameters such as land area and circuit breaker
counts. We estimated these costs using typical parameters for substations of this voltage class
(see Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Table 5 for billing items, unit costs, and
assumptions).
Construction and substation costs for UGC AC and their corresponding capacities were
derived from the 2025 IET report37. For gas-insulated lines (GIL), we referenced the construction
parameters of China’s Su-Tong 1000 kV GIL corridor, with a total cost of 4.763 billion CNY. As
specific cost breakdowns were unavailable, we estimated substation/terminal station costs at 16–
26% of the total, based on similar projects. This portion covers terminal station construction,
auxiliary systems, and project management. Terminal stations ensure seamless integration
between GIL and ultra-high-voltage overhead lines. We used a mid-range estimate of 1.013
billion CNY for these costs.
Lifecycle costs were evaluated over the full operational lifespan of each system. AC and
DC overhead lines were assigned a conservative lifecycle of 30 years, reflecting the minimum
expected duration in challenging mountainous regions61. Underground AC cables have a 30-year
lifecycle, while the tunnels themselves have a minimum lifespan of 50 years. Thus, cable and
tunnel costs were calculated separately, with cables and tunnels accounting for 42.5% and 57.5%
of total costs, respectively, as per the IET report37. For GIL, both the lines and tunnels have a 50-
year lifecycle. Although lifetimes differ by component (OHL: 30 years; UGC cable: 30 years;
tunnels and GIL: 50 years), all costs are annualized consistently over their respective service lives
within the LCC framework.
Operation and maintenance costs for AC overhead lines were estimated at 5% of
construction costs annually62. For DC overhead lines, this was set at 1% per year43. Underground
tunnel maintenance costs are lower relative to construction costs, at approximately 0.5%
annually62. Another study suggests AC overhead and UGC maintenance costs are 1.5% and 0.15%
of construction costs, respectively63, confirming UGC costs rate are roughly one-tenth of AC
overhead lines. Due to limited data on GIL maintenance, we assumed the same 0.5% of
construction costs as UGC AC.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper analyzes and anticipates underground tunnel power transmission technology as a promising candidate to the problem of transporting energy from mountainous regions. The performances of overhead line, underground cable, as well as GIL are discussed, such as costs, electromagnetic safety, et al. However, overall, the conclusions in this paper still need to be further verified, and some analysis methods used in this paper are lack of credibility.
1.In Table I, it is recognized that the ecological cost, public opinion cost and climatic disaster loss of UGC and GIL are all zero. Obviously, it is too arbitrary and idealized. For example, the underground cable is also affected by the natural disaster, such as floods, earthquakes, mudslides.
2.Correspondingly, the conclusion that “with a typical typical transmission line life cycle of 40 years, underground transmission tunnels will even be 72.4% cheaper than overhead transmission lines.” looks beyond normal cognition. If this conclusion is right, all of the overhead line should be replaced by the underground tunnels. But actually, most of the high voltage transmission uses the overhead line.
3.Similarly, it is claimed that “the 1,000 kV GIL can carry roughly six times the power capacity of a 500 kV XLPE cable, commercially available cable solution under state-of-art technology level. Under conditions demanding high-density, large-capacity transmission, GIL technology therefore may offer superior overall cost-effectiveness.” This conclusion is very arbitrary and lack of theoretical support. The authors hope to obtain the conclusion underground cable of GIL is better than overhead line for large capacity and long distance transmission. This is contrary to objective facts.
4.What is the main innovation of this paper? This manuscript looks like an analysis report, while not a scientific paper.
5.In addition, the dc transmission technology should also be discussed. Because compared with ac transmission, HVDC system is more suitable for long-distance transmission.

## Abstract

Mountainous regions, such as the Alps, Appalachians, Andes, and Qingzang Plateau, offer
vast renewable energy potential, but geographical and ecological challenges limit conventional
overhead transmission lines. Underground alternatives, including gas-insulated lines and cables,
provide viable solutions but require comprehensive techno-economic evaluation for sustainable

and fluid dynamics, with lifecycle cost assessment per unit transmission task to compare
overhead and underground tunnel transmission systems. Optimized conductor designs and
ventilation strategies enhance cable capacity and improvRe economic performance, particularly in
regions with high external costs. Here, we sh ow that underground tunnel based power
transmission systems, especially gas-insulIated lines, deliver cost-effective, high-capacity
transmission solutions for mountainous renewable energy concentrated regions, outperform
overhead power transmission infrastructure when external costs, including ecological, landscape,
and infrastructure constraRints, are significant, thus advancing the goals of sustainable renewable
energy integration and net-zero.

## Introduction

Facing the global energy crisis and increasing urgency of transitioning towards a low-
carbon future1,2, effective utilization of renewable energy has become crucial. By 2027, the global
renewable energy generation capacity is projected to increase by approximately 2,400 GW3. The
capacity and type of renewable energy construction expected to be completed by 2027 in
countries/regions around the world is provided in Supplementary Figure 1. A critical challenge
in realizing this growth lies in transmitting power from remote, resource-rich regions to demand
centers, ensuring feasibility, stability, and alignment with environmental policies and public
expectations4.
Untapped renewable energy resources are particularly concentrated in mountainous and
highland regions5,6, where elevated terrain enhances solar irradiance7, wind speeds8, and
hydropower potential. Other areas, such as offshore wind sites, also represent globally significant
resources, but the present study focuses on mountainous and plateau regions where corridor
scarcity and ecological sensitivity are especially pronounced. However, these areas frequently
overlap with ecologically sensitive or scenic regions9,10. For example, the Appalachian Mountains
in eastern North America hold an estimated 1,859 GW of wind power generation capacity
potential11, while the Andes in South America possess about 243 GW of combined wind and
geothermal generation capacity potential12. The NEuropean Alps offer 19.9 GW of wind generation
capacity potential, 45 GW of solar generat ion capacity potential, and 8.56 GW of hydropower
generation capacity potential8. In Chin L a, the Qingzang Plateau is targeted for the development of
227 GW of hydropower generation capacity and 96 GW of photovoltaic generation capacity13–15.
Indonesia’s Central Range (New Guinea Highlands) contains approximately 26 GW of renewable
generation capacity potential, most of which is hydropower, leveraging the area’s rugged terrain16.
These figures, which are shown in Table 1, are based on regional studies that report only partial,
technically proven reserves rather than the full exploitable potential of each mountain range.
Although the methodologies differ—ranging from geographic information system-based spatial
analysis to hydrological modeling—they consistently highlight the vast untapped renewable
potential of these regions17,18.
However, transmitting renewable energy from these areas faces significant challenges:
Geographical and Corridor Constraints: Mountainous regions require long-distance exports to
lowland load centers, yet feasible overhead corridors are sharply limited by rugged terrain and
regulatory siting restrictions. On the Qingzang Plateau, for instance, four planned transmission
pathways (northern, southern, central, and central-branch) intersect with multiple nature reserves,
leaving only ~16 feasible HV circuits compared to ~37 required for the planned renewable
buildout (≈40% realizable via OHL)19,20. Comparable potential corridor scarcity exists in the
Alps, where Natura 2000 and UNESCO sites restrict routing options, and in the Appalachians,
where national forests and the Appalachian Trail limit siting flexibility. Ecological and Tourism
Protection: Beyond technical siting limits, these mountain regions also carry exceptional
ecological and scenic value21. Overhead lines fragment habitats and impair landscapes, triggering
strong public opposition. In the Alps, willingness-to-pay (WTP) studies indicate more than
$900,000 per kilometer per year to undergroun d lines, reflecting the premium placed on
preserving biodiversity and visual integrity 22,23.
For decades, traditional overLhead transmission lines (OHL) have dominated power
delivery, yet they inadequately address these challenges in renewable-rich mountainous and
plateau scenarios. This Rhas spurred exploration of alternatives, with underground tunnel
transmission emerging as a viable solution for long-distance, high-capacity power transport.
Unlike OHL, tunnels bypass surface constraints and ecological impacts, enabling delivery
through challenging terrains while preserving landscapes24,25. The undergrounding alternatives
include direct-buried and tunnel installations; while direct burial is generally cheaper, in
mountainous, corridor-scarce, and environmentally sensitive segments, continuous trenching is
often infeasible and operators therefore typically adopt accessible cable tunnels for bulk
transmission25.
However, applying underground transmission tunnel technologies—such as cross-linked
polyethylene (XLPE) AC or DC cables or higher-voltage gas-insulated lines (GIL)—to
renewable-rich regions presents multiple unresolved challenges26. First, economic costs are a
primary concern. Although, studies have quantified the additional ecological and landscape costs
of overhead transmission lines (OHLs) and the economic benefits of undergrounding, clear
criteria and guidelines for determining which regions should prioritize underground solutions
versus OHLs, based on regional characteristics, remain absent. Second, the design of current-
carrying capacity for lines within tunnels has been evaluated by finite element analysis,
accounting for electromagnetic and thermal coupling27–30. However, few studies have
investigated how the spatial arrangement of lines within tunnels impacts their current-carrying
capacity31. Third, ventilation is critical for maintaining eRnvironmental stability in long, confined
tunnel spaces. Previous research has proposed vent ilation strategies for cable tunnels using finite
element analysis32, and a recent study oIptimized ventilation by constraining conductor
temperatures and factoring in energy loss costs33,34. However, this work was limited to a single-
tunnel scenario and focused solely on reducing ventilation energy losses, without exploring the
coupled relationship between ventilation and current-carrying capacity in long-distance tunnels.
Furthermore, current research has not sufficiently elucidated the interplay between multi-physics
fields—encompassing electromagnetic, thermal, and fluid dynamics—and economic benefits in
critical tunnel design aspects, such as line layout and ventilation. This gap hinders the
development of comprehensive design guidelines and economic evaluation frameworks for long-
distance tunnel transmission in mountainous regions.
In this work, we present a comprehensive framework for evaluating underground tunnel
transmission in renewable-rich mountainous and plateau scenarios, delivering three key
contributions: (1) A multi-physics coupling methodology integrating electromagnetic-thermal-
fluid finite element analysis with annualized lifecycle cost (LCC) per unit transmission task
(MW-km) evaluation, enabling rigorous comparison of GIL, UGC AC, and UGC DC under
realistic constraints. (2) A techno-economic model that accounts for ecological and landscape
costs, demonstrating that underground solutions, particularly GIL, achieve lower annualized LCC
per unit transmission task (MW-km) than overhead lines when external costs exceed
$550,000/km/year, redefining economic feasibility for renewable energy transmission in
mountainous regions worldwide. (3) Quantitative insights into spatial and ventilation
optimizations, demonstrating up to 57% capacity enhancements (e.g., AC cables from 1,273 A to
2,003 A) and 20% LCC savings in annualized LCC per unit transmission task (MW-km) via
parameterized simulations, providing actionable design gRuidelines for sustainable energy delivery.
This framework equips policymakers and engineers with a decision-support matrix, accelerating
deployment of underground tunnels to uInlock mountainous renewables, foster net-zero
transitions, and balance economic, environmental, and social imperatives.

## Results

Comparative Techno-Economic Evaluation of Transmission Technologies for Renewable
Energy Concentrated Zones
To evaluate the economic viability of various high-capacity power transmission methods,
we analyzed alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) overhead lines (OHL), underground
tunnel AC cables (UGC AC), and gas-insulated lines (GIL).
We selected 500 kV AC and ±600 kV DC overhead lines as benchmarks, as these are
widely adopted and technologically mature transmission systems. Cost data for these lines were
sourced from the 2024 MISO handbook, which provides U.S. power infrastructure construction
costs, with the tower type specified as an angled dead-end structure, suitable for mountainous
and high-altitude regions rich in renewable energy35. While China has implemented mature 1,000
kV AC and ±1,000 kV DC overhead lines with estimated costs of approximately $3,802,580/km
and $1,801,444/km, respectively, these data stem from specific projects and the technologies are
less commonly applied globally36. Thus, they are excluded from the main analysis but provided
in Supplementary Table 1 for reference.
For underground tunnel AC transmission, construction costs were derived from the 2025
IET report on underground cable systems37. Because published cost data for long tunnel GIL
systems remain scarce, we explicitly note that the Su-Tong GIL corridor is a short river-crossing
tunnel (Yangtze crossing) and use it as a conservative reference , while Supplementary Tables 1–
2 compile additional project data (including an Chinese GRIL tunnel) to broaden the evidence base.
Operation and maintenance costs were estimated based on industry averages and multiple
research reports. The Su-Tong GIL project haIs a rated current of 6,300 A. However, based on a
State Grid Corporation of China report and our subsequent studies38, dual-circuit lines operate at
a reduced current of 3,150 A under normal conditions to maintain stable tunnel temperatures.
Therefore, the capacity calculations are based on 3,150 A. Energy loss data for AC and DC
overhead lines were obtained from EIA report39. For UGC AC and GIL, where empirical loss
data are scarce, we conducted coupled electromagnetic-thermal-fluidic finite element analysis,
estimating energy losses of 11.91%/1,000 km for UGC AC and 6.71%/1,000 km for GIL
(Calculation details are shown in the Methods Section). These numbers align closely with
industry expectations and also with the data we collected from State Grid Corporation of China,
which is 15.2%/1,000 km and 5.96%/1,000 km for UGC AC and GIL, respectively. The data are
given in Supplementary Table 2.
Transmission lines in renewable-rich mountainous regions often traverse ecologically
sensitive or scenic areas, where OHLs significantly impact ecosystems and aesthetic value40. To
quantify these costs, we adopted the willingness-to-pay (WTP) metric, using the Alps as a case.
Two studies reported residents’ WTP for undergrounding overhead lines in the Alps at
$984,000/year/km and $892,043/year/km, respectively. We used their average, $938,022/year/km,
for cost estimation22,41.
Although we also investigated underground DC transmission, limited case studies and
data availability constrained the cost analysis. However, we posit that its costs are comparable to
underground AC cables, as both primarily incur additional expenses from tunnel construction and
equipment installation compared to overhead lines.
Table 2 summarizes the economic cost data for thRese transmission methods. Although the
data are drawn from diverse countries, projects, and studies, it still serves a reliable reference for
comparative analysis.
To determine the most suitable transmission method for renewable energy-rich regions,
we evaluated lifecycle unit capacity costs, analyzing total and per-unit-length costs as a function
of transmission distance, which is shown in Fig. 1.
Ecological and landscape costs constitute a significant portion of overhead line expenses,
particularly in sensitive regions like the Alps. These costs vary by region, so we plotted cost
curves with and without ecological considerations. When including ecological costs, overhead
lines exhibit the highest lifecycle unit costs: approximately $430/year/MW/km (DC) and
$400/year/MW/km (AC) at a 500 km distance. Underground AC cables follow at
$321/year/MW/km, and GIL at $263/year/MW/km.
Excluding ecological costs, overhead lines are significantly cheaper, with costs of
$33/year/MW/km (DC) and $28/year/MW/km (AC). Thus, without ecological costs, GIL costs
are roughly 8 times higher than overhead lines, and costs for underground AC cables are
approximately ten times higher. When ecological costs are excluded, overhead AC lines are more
cost-effective for distances below 800 km, while DC lines become preferable beyond 800 km.
This aligns with trends in prior studies42.
Acknowledging that infrastructure costs—particularly tunnel excavation—are highly
project-specific and dependent on local geological conditions, we conducted a comprehensive
sensitivity analysis to validate the robustness of our economic model. We evaluated the impact
of cost variations across three key dimensions: tunnel civil engineering costs (ranging from −50%
to +100% to cover geological complexities), electrical equipment costs, and operation and
maintenance expenses43. The detailed parameter settinRgs and the resulting sensitivity analysis
(presented as a tornado diagram) are provided in Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary
Figure 2. The results demonstrate that the Ieconomic advantage of GIL is resilient to cost
uncertainties; even under scenarios of significantly higher tunnel construction costs (e.g., in
complex terrain), the GIL system remains a cost-competitive alternative to overhead lines when
high ecological externalities are factored in.
The choice between overhead and underground solutions hinges on ecological, landscape,
and other external costs, such as additional expenses for constructing new lines in fully occupied
corridors, forest clearing, ecological fees, and steep terrain construction. Further analysis reveals
that when these external costs reach $550,000/km/year, overhead lines’ unit costs approach those
of GIL; at $720,000/km/year, they align with underground AC cables. Therefore, we conclude
that underground GIL systems become more cost-effective when external costs exceed
$550,000/km/year in target regions, offering a viable alternative for sustainable, high-capacity
power transmission.
Electromagnetic Safety Analysis of Transmission Technologies in Underground Tunnels
Electromagnetic safety is a critical consideration for underground tunnels housing high-
voltage equipment. The confined geometry and proximity of conductors, maintenance personnel,
and surrounding infrastructure necessitate rigorous evaluation of electric and magnetic field
distributions to ensure operational safety and compliance with regulations44.
Following IEEE standards, occupational exposure limits for 50 Hz AC magnetic fields
are 2,710 μT and electric fields are 5 kV/m; for DC, magnetic fields are limited to 353,000 μT
and electric fields are limited to 5 kV/m (based on stricter head-exposure criteria)45,46. ICNIRP
standards limit electric fields to 10 kV/m and magnetic fields to 1,000 μT for AC 50Hz47. For this
analysis, we adopt the stricter standards: AC (50 Hz): 5 kV/m, 1,000 μT; DC: 5 kV/m, 353,000
μT.
For electric fields, both XLPE cablIes (AC and DC) and gas-insulated lines (GIL)
incorporate grounded shielding layers or enclosures, resulting in external electric fields near zero
during normal operation. However, it is crucial to distinguish normal operation from fault
conditions. While the aRforementioned shielding is effective under steady-state scenarios,
insulation breakdowns—though relatively infrequent with typical failure rates of approximately
0.1 to 0.5 failures per 100 km·year for modern high-voltage systems —pose a different set of
risks. In the event of an insulation fault, short-circuit currents (often reaching tens of kA) will
flow through the cable sheath. Without proper mitigation, this massive current induces significant
longitudinal voltages along the sheath, creating life-threatening touch potentials at the cable
surface. To mitigate this risk, we recommend the installation of Sheath Voltage Limiters (SVLs)
within the system—typically at cross-bonding points—to clamp potential overvoltages to safe
levels. Additionally, implementing an equipotential grounding grid throughout the tunnel is
advised. These measures ensure that the tunnel environment remains safe for maintenance
personnel access.
A more common scenario involves partially grounded shielding due to distant grounding
points. Simulations indicate that with a shielding layer voltage of approximately 1 V, the electric
field at 0.1 m from the conductor is about 3.76 V/m, well below safety thresholds. These
simulation results are detailed in Supplementary Figure 3. For these simulations, excitation
voltages were 500 kV (AC XLPE), 500 kV (DC XLPE), and 1,000 kV (GIL), with currents of
2,000 A (AC), 2,000 A (DC), and 6,000 A (GIL). Thus, electric field intensities and touch
potentials in tunnels are controllable and safe through the combination of conductor shielding
and fault protection measures.
Magnetic field analysis is complex due to the influence of multi-phase conductor
arrangements and shielding interconnection mIethods. We conducted magnetic field simulations
in tunnel environments, evaluating AC and DC cables in circular and square tunnels with stacked
and wall-mounted configurations (see Supplementary Figure 4 for schematics and dimensions).
For GIL, we analyzed the tunnel configuration of the Su-Tong GIL corridor 38 (Supplementary
Figure 5).
Regarding shielding grounding methods, DC cable shielding does not produce induced
voltage due to the absence of time-varying currents, allowing solid bonding48. GIL enclosures,
designed as continuous conductors to carry the return current, significantly reduce external
magnetic fields and transmission losses, typically employing solid bonding or multiple-point
bonding rather than cross-bonding. In contrast, long-distance AC XLPE cables, due to high
shielding losses, generally use cross-bonding. In our tunnel model simulations, DC cable
shielding and GIL enclosures use solid bonding, while AC cable shielding employs cross-bonding.
Magnetic field intensity distributions in tunnel environments are shown in Fig. 2.
In tunnels, GIL exhibits the lowest external magnetic field intensity, posing no health risks
unless directly contacting the conductor surface. DC cables produce higher magnetic fields,
approximately 500 μT within 0.6 m, but these remain well below the DC safety limit of 353,000
μT. AC cables show significantly higher magnetic fields, exceeding 1,000 μT within a 0.3 m
radius for both stacked and wall-mounted configurations. Simulation results suggest that wall-
mounted configurations allow maintenance personnel to avoid high-intensity magnetic fields in
the tunnel’s central walkway. For stacked configurations, placing conductors entirely along
tunnel walls is preferable to minimize exposure.
Spatial Configuration Effects on Power Loss and Thermal Performance in Underground
Tunnels
The operation of transmission syste ms in tunnel environments differs significantly from
overhead lines due to the confined, elongated space with limited heat dissipation49. A primary
challenge is balancing increased current-carrying capacity—enhancing economic value—with
the pronounced thermal effects it induces. Excessive heat, causing conductor temperatures to
exceed 90°C for XLPE cables (or 105°C for GIL)38, reduces conductor lifespan. Variations in
conductor spatial arrangements influence power loss and temperature through magnetic field
coupling and altered heat dissipation structures. To investigate these effects, we conducted finite
element analysis on the impact of conductor spatial arrangements on temperature and power loss
for three tunnel configurations.
We defined spatial parameters based on installation methods: for stacked cable
configurations, L represents the distance between the centers of two circuits; for GIL, L
denotes the horizontal distance between circuits. In square wall-mounted and GIL scenarios, H
indicates the vertical distance between adjacent conductors within the same circuit. In circular
wall-mounted scenarios,  represents the angle between the line connecting the topmost
conductor to the tunnel center and the horizontal axis. These parameters are illustrated in
Supplementary Figure 4. The resulting conductor temperature variations and tunnel thermal
losses are shown in Fig. 3.
For AC cables in stacked configurations with fixed intra-phase distances, increasing the
inter-circuit distance (L) has minimal impact on power loss but reduces conductor temperature.
In circular stacked scenarios, total losses increase slightly from 345 W/m (L = 0.4 m) to 347
W/m ( L = 1.4 m), while temperature decreases from 131.02°C to 126.42°C. In square stacked
scenarios, losses rise from 338 W/m ( L = 0.4 m) to 344 W/m ( L = 1.5 m), with temperature
dropping from 125.41°C to 121.86°C. This indicates that increasing the distance between heat
sources slightly increases losses (primarily shielding layer losses, with conductor losses
unchanged) but enhances heat dissipation, lowering conductor temperature and slightly
increasing current-carrying capacity from 1,273 A to 1,304 A (circular) and 1,310 A to 1,335 A
(square). In wall-mounted configurations, increasing intra-circuit conductor distance
significantly reduces shielding layer losses, from 64 W/m to 2 W/m (circular) and 88 W/m to 3
W/m (square), boosting current-carrying capacity by over 200 A in both scenarios. Further
analysis attributes this to the cross-bonding shielding method used, where larger intra-phase
distances allow balanced three-phase induced currents to neutralize shielding layer currents,
reducing losses. For AC cables, I²R losses dominate across all configurations. In stacked
configurations, shielding layer losses are significant (64–88 W/m, ~18–25% of total losses of
338–347 W/m), despite mitigation by cross-bonding. In wall-mounted configurations, shielding
layer losses drop to 2–3 W/m, making I²R losses even more dominant. AC cables exhibit higher
I²R losses than DC cables due to two factors: (1) shielding layer losses increase conductor
temperature, raising resistance, and (2) skin effect increases effective conductor resistance.
Simulations using a uniform multi-turn conductor model (single turn) estimate I²R losses without
skin effect at 168.37 W/m, compared to 235.63 W/m with skin effect, indicating a skin effect
contribution of ~67.26 W/m (~19% of stacked losses, ~32% of minimum wall-mounted losses).
Note that skin effect is a component of I²R losses, manifesting as increased resistance.
For DC cables, the static magnetic field eliminates shielding layer induced currents and
associated thermal losses, as well as AC-specific skin effects, resulting in lower losses and
temperatures compared to AC cables, unaffected by spatial arrangement. However, increasing
heat source distance improves dissipation, slightly raisiRng current-carrying capacity from 2,605
A, 2,658 A, 2,655 A, and 2,668 A to 2,663 A, 2,6 84 A, 2,714 A, and 2,710 A across the four
scenarios, with increases ranging from 26 A tIo 59 A. For DC cables, I²R losses are the sole loss
mechanism, as shielding layer losses and skin effect are absent.
For GIL, prior magnetic environment analysis shows low external magnetic fields and
minimal inter-phase coupling due to larger line distances, resulting in negligible power loss
changes with spatial arrangement. Capacity increases, driven by improved heat dissipation from
increased L and H , are modest, from 4,411 A to 4,466 A. For GIL, I²R losses dominate (976–

aligning with the data from a Sutong GIL related reference50. Skin effect contributes ~11% of

significantly enhance AC cable current-carrying capacity, reducing power loss and allowing
increases from 1,273 A to 2,003 A under temperature constraints. For DC cables, the absence of
induced currents limits the impact of spatial changes, and for GIL, low external fields and large
distances minimize loss variations, with capacity gains primarily from improved heat dissipation.
These findings provide a clear guidance for tunnel based power transmission design for
renewable energy dispatch from energy concentrated zones.

## Methods

Lifecycle cost analysis
To assess the economic viability of powerP transmission systems, we calculated the
construction costs of transmission lines and substations separately. For new lines, we assumed
the need for substations or converter stations at both ends to match the line’s capacity.
For 500 kV AC and ±600 kV DC overhead lines, construction and substation/converter
station costs, including operation and maintenance, were sourced from the 2024 MISO report35.
For AC substations, the report requires additional parameters such as land area and circuit breaker
counts. We estimated these costs using typical parameters for substations of this voltage class
(see Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Table 5 for billing items, unit costs, and
assumptions).
Construction and substation costs for UGC AC and their corresponding capacities were
derived from the 2025 IET report37. For gas-insulated lines (GIL), we referenced the construction
parameters of China’s Su-Tong 1000 kV GIL corridor, with a total cost of 4.763 billion CNY. As
specific cost breakdowns were unavailable, we estimated substation/terminal station costs at 16–
26% of the total, based on similar projects. This portion covers terminal station construction,
auxiliary systems, and project management. Terminal stations ensure seamless integration
between GIL and ultra-high-voltage overhead lines. We used a mid-range estimate of 1.013
billion CNY for these costs.
Lifecycle costs were evaluated over the full operational lifespan of each system. AC and
DC overhead lines were assigned a conservative lifecycle of 30 years, reflecting the minimum
expected duration in challenging mountainous regions61. Underground AC cables have a 30-year
lifecycle, while the tunnels themselves have a minimum lifespan of 50 years. Thus, cable and
tunnel costs were calculated separately, with cables and tunnels accounting for 42.5% and 57.5%
of total costs, respectively, as per the IET report37. For GIL, both the lines and tunnels have a 50-
year lifecycle. Although lifetimes differ by component (OHL: 30 years; UGC cable: 30 years;
tunnels and GIL: 50 years), all costs are annualized consistently over their respective service lives
within the LCC framework.
Operation and maintenance costs for AC overhead lines were estimated at 5% of
construction costs annually62. For DC overhead lines, this was set at 1% per year43. Underground
tunnel maintenance costs are lower relative to construction costs, at approximately 0.5%
annually62. Another study suggests AC overhead and UGC maintenance costs are 1.5% and 0.15%
of construction costs, respectively63, confirming UGC costs rate are roughly one-tenth of AC
overhead lines. Due to limited data on GIL maintenance, we assumed the same 0.5% of
construction costs as UGC AC.

This paper analyzes and anticipates underground tunnel power transmission technology as a promising candidate to the problem of transporting energy from mountainous regions. The performances of overhead line, underground cable, as well as GIL are discussed, such as costs, electromagnetic safety, et al. However, overall, the conclusions in this paper still need to be further verified, and some analysis methods used in this paper are lack of credibility.
